The renewal was disclosed in a release issued on Thursday, November fifth, and the program allows share on either venue. The announcement also offers context for market participants tracking the S&P/TSX Composite Index.

An ATM program is a standing facility rather than a single financing. It does not commit the company to issue any shares at all. Instead, it allows Cameco to release new stock into the open market in increments, at prevailing prices, whenever management judges it useful. The company stated that any will take place at its discretion.

The program remains in effect until early December, a little more than three years from the renewal date, unless the full amount is issued sooner or the agreement is terminated earlier. Because the shares are released at market prices rather than at a negotiated discount, ATM structures are often used by large issuers that want flexibility without the price concession typical of an overnight bought deal. The timing and size of any are at the company's discretion and are disclosed as activity occurs.

The facility sits under a base shelf prospectus that permits Cameco to offer up to three billion U.S. dollars of securities over a thirty-seven-month period. For U.S. a prospectus supplement was filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. In Canada, the shelf system allows a seasoned issuer to qualify securities once and then draw on that qualification through supplements, with continuous disclosure documents available on SEDAR+.

sum: Cameco's stock slipped 2.8% in the latest session, a move that coincided with BMO Capital reiterating its Buy rating and a C$150 price target. Yet the more telling signal for investors sits in the fine print of the uranium producer's third-quarter filing rather than in any broker note.

The headline numbers from the 30 October report look reassuring enough: a net profit of C$43 million for Q3 2026. Strip out the adjustments, though, and Cameco booked a net loss of C$2 million. Adjusted EBITDA came in at C$267 million. That gap between reported and underlying earnings is the lens through which the rest of the quarter should be read.

Management pinned the weak adjusted result on a trio of pressures — an extended scheduled maintenance shutdown at Key Lake, lower sales volumes, and higher average unit costs. All three feed directly into the question of whether the company can convert its improved outlook into actual cash generation.

Cameco used the quarterly release to narrow its 2026 uranium production forecast to 19.5–20.5 million pounds. The ceiling came down from 21.5 million pounds while the floor held steady, giving a tighter but lower-topped range. Sales and deliveries guidance was also compressed, to 29.5–30.5 million pounds from a prior 29–32 million pounds — a narrower band with a raised floor and a trimmed top.

A tighter range is only as good as its execution. With maintenance overhang, volumes and unit costs all weighing on the quarter, the credibility of that guidance will be settled on the operational side, not in the forecast document itself.

Analyst sentiment has been moving in a constructive direction even as targets shift. Paradigm upgraded Cameco to Buy on Monday while trimming its price target to C$130 — a combination that pairs confidence in the equity with tempered expectations for the business. BMO's C$150 target, reaffirmed alongside its Buy rating, sits at the more optimistic end of the range.

On 5 November Cameco renewed its at-the-market equity programme, giving it discretion to issue up to US$1 billion of common shares. A separate shelf registration permits securities offerings totalling up to US$3 billion over 37 months.

Oklo (NASDAQ: OKLO) shed 13% in a single day, while Bloom Energy cratered 16%, as markets repriced the assumption that a hyperscaler-driven electricity boom would underpin the entire sector.
The selloff exposed a fundamental question: how much of the nuclear investment case actually depends on data centers, and how much was always about something else entirely?
Cameco (NYSE: CCJ) CEO Timothy Gitzel addressed that question directly on his company’s third-quarter earnings call, drawing a clear line between the AI narrative and his firm’s core business model.

“Artificial intelligence and data centers can provide meaningful upside, but they are not the foundation of the nuclear investment thesis nor are they a load-bearing assumption in our strategy,” Gitzel said.
His argument rests on contracted fuel demand from reactors already generating power today, a base that continues burning uranium regardless of what hyperscalers decide to build next quarter.
Cameco had 230 million pounds of uranium committed across 39 customers at the close of 2025, providing revenue visibility that few companies in the sector can match.

sum: Cameco has moved on two fronts at once — shareholder returns and balance-sheet firepower — while stressing that a fresh technical report for its flagship Saskatchewan mine reflects no change to the underlying resource.

The uranium producer confirmed a 2026 annual dividend of C$0.24 per common share, payable December 15 to holders of record as of November 30. Alongside that payout, it has lodged a shelf prospectus and registration statement enabling securities offerings worth up to US$3 billion over 37 months.

The financing architecture also includes a renewed at-the-market equity program, which gives Cameco discretion to issue common shares worth up to US$1 billion, or the equivalent in Canadian dollars. The company was explicit that it is under no obligation to sell any stock under the arrangement, and the prior distribution agreement has been terminated.
For existing holders, the program cuts both ways: it keeps capital access open at times of management's choosing, but any drawdown would dilute the current share base.

Separately, Cameco filed an updated NI 43-101 technical report for McArthur River on Wednesday. Management described the submission as voluntary, aimed at refreshing information on the operation rather than reflecting any material change to mineral reserves or resources.

The operational backdrop against which these decisions land is more mixed. Third-quarter 2026 results, reported October 30, showed a net profit of C$43 million, yet the adjusted figure was a loss of C$2 million. Adjusted EBITDA came in at C$267 million.

The gap between the headline and adjusted numbers traces to a planned extended maintenance shutdown at Key Lake, which curtailed output and pushed costs higher. Whether that drag proves temporary is the operative question — an easing in production and cost pressure once maintenance wraps up would support the earnings case, while a prolonged effect would not.

Cameco Stock Fell After Earnings: Europe’s Nuclear Push Could Matter More Over 10 Years
sum: Europe's nuclear ambitions offer a longer view beyond the shares of one company falling over a couple months. Reactors operating for decades need fuel long after a few bad quarters, and Canada already has a company selling into that market.

Nuclear power can help an electricity system produce dependable output without the direct carbon emissions of burning fossil fuels. That makes it relevant to Europe's combined interest in energy security and lower emissions. Friday's summit included nuclear cooperation within a wider energy relationship, adding policy support to an industry that already has working reactors and customers.

The commercial opportunity isn't limited to building a new reactor. Existing plants need replacement fuel, maintenance, and services to keep operating. Life extensions can lengthen that demand. For investors, that creates an earnings opportunity tied to assets already producing electricity, with new construction providing another possible source of growth over a much longer period.

Long-term fuel agreements also make uranium different from a business selling every unit at today's quoted commodity price. Contract terms and delivery schedules influence when stronger market conditions reach earnings. A disappointing quarter can therefore coexist with a sound customer outlook. It still needs explaining, particularly when production problems or rising costs are taking away part of the benefit.

Cameco (TSX: CCO) produces uranium, provides fuel services, and participates in reactor technology and services through its Westinghouse ownership. Its Slovak fuel-supply agreement extends to 2036. That gives the European connection substance beyond a new summit statement. Customers have already made commitments connected to keeping their nuclear operations supplied over many years.

Chief executive Tim Gitzel said the company won't pursue growth "simply in response to headlines." I like that discipline in a commodity business. Production requires capital and dependable operations, while an attractive customer commitment can provide a better reason to spend. A nuclear theme becomes more investable when management keeps the eventual return ahead of the excitement.

sum: Cameco's stock has lagged uranium's record rally even as the metal hits a 19 year high. The culprit was the company's own numbers: a badly missed earnings quarter and a lowered production forecast.

Shares of Cameco trade near $85 in early October, even as the metal it mines keeps getting pricier. The reason isn't some disconnect in the uranium market. In its most recent quarterly report, the world's largest publicly traded uranium producer posted earnings of 5 cents a share, badly missing the 28 cents analysts had expected, as revenue fell nearly 15% from a year earlier. Cameco also cut its production forecast at the McArthur River/Key Lake operation to between 14 million and 15 million pounds, down from the 18 million pounds it had guided to earlier in the year, citing delays in transitioning to new mining areas. The stock took a further hit after July 1, when the company temporarily suspended its Cigar Lake mine in Saskatchewan over problems at Orano's McClean Lake mill, the facility that processes Cigar Lake's ore.

Here's the part that actually confused people: uranium itself has never been pricier in nearly two decades. Cameco's own data stretches back to 1996. It shows the average long-term contract price climbing to its highest level in nearly two decades, a run consistent with the metal's strongest stretch since the mid-2000s boom. Spot uranium has also traded at multi-year highs this year. So the question making the rounds among investors was simple: if the stuff Cameco digs up and sells is worth more than it's been in a generation, why is Cameco's stock going the other way?

The answer is that Cameco doesn't sell much uranium at the spot price. Its business runs on long-term contracts signed years in advance. Many are priced well below what the market pays today, which is exactly why the company's realized price lagged the headline numbers even as spot and term prices climbed. Add a mine that briefly stopped producing. Add a mill run by a different company that had its own problems. Add a production forecast that just got cut. A stock price doesn't need a conspiracy to explain why it fell. It needs an earnings report. Wall Street had been pricing Cameco partly on the assumption that rising uranium would show up cleanly in its numbers quarter after quarter.

sum: Cameco Corporation CCJ has confirmed that operations at the Cigar Lake uranium mine and Orano's McClean Lake mill have resumed and reinforced confidence in its 2026 output targets. The restart follows a temporary suspension announced earlier this month due to operational issues at the McClean Lake mill, where all Cigar Lake ore is processed.

The disruption stemmed from problems at the mill's sulfuric acid plant, which was forced to be shut down for repairs. The McClean Lake mill has now resumed operations. Cigar Lake has begun shipping stockpiled ore to the mill and has restarted production at the mine.
Despite the roughly two-week interruption, Cameco expects no impact on the mine's annual production guidance of 17.5-18.0 million pounds on a 100% basis.

Cigar Lake remains one of Cameco's most strategic assets. Located in northern Saskatchewan, Canada, the mine is renowned for its exceptionally high-grade uranium ore and long reserve life, making it one of the world's premier uranium operations. Cameco recently strengthened its position by increasing its ownership stake in the mine by 2.871 percentage points to 57.418%.

In 2025, the mine produced 19.1 million pounds, with Cameco's attributable share at 10.4 million pounds. Under its previous 54.547% ownership, the company had projected attributable 2026 production of 9.5-10.0 million pounds. Following the recent increase in ownership, the company is expected to update its attributable production outlook to reflect the same.

The Cigar Lake restart marks the second operational challenge Cameco has successfully navigated this year. In May, the company temporarily suspended operations at its McArthur River mine and Key Lake mill after severe flooding in northern Saskatchewan caused a partial collapse of the Smoothstone River Bridge, a critical transportation route used to deliver supplies to the sites. Cameco quickly established an alternative logistics route, restoring the flow of essential materials and enabling both operations to return to full production within a short period.
Importantly, that disruption also left Cameco's production outlook unchanged.

sum: Canada’s leading uranium producer Cameco (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) has sealed a joint acquisition with France’s Orano to purchase the full 5% joint venture stake previously owned by TEPCO Resources in the world’s top-tier high-grade Cigar Lake uranium mine, locking up complete control of the core mineral asset. The company’s aggressive bet on its flagship mine coincides with a steep retreat in its share price, and booming nuclear power demand spurred by large-scale AI data centre construction has made the stock’s contrarian investment potential a hot topic among market participants.

Per an official corporate release published on Monday, Cameco and Orano split TEPCO’s 5% equity holding unevenly: Cameco acquired a 2.871% interest and Orano secured the leftover 2.129%. Once the transaction wraps up, Cameco’s ownership in Cigar Lake will rise to 57.418% and Orano’s stake will reach 42.582%, turning the long-term business partners into the mine’s exclusive holders. Cameco paid C$115.75 million, equivalent to US$83.6 million, for its portion of the deal, while Orano’s investment cost has not been disclosed. The whole transaction is scheduled to finalize in the third quarter of 2026.

Sited roughly 660 kilometres north of Saskatoon in Saskatchewan, the Cigar Lake uranium deposit was uncovered in the early 1980s and kicked off formal production in 2014 with Cameco acting as the mine operator. The two miners have built long-standing cooperative ties beyond Cigar Lake, co-managing the McArthur River uranium mine and Key Lake mill located within the same Canadian province. TEPCO later joined the project as a minority stakeholder and will fully exit the partnership upon the deal’s completion. Cameco’s chief executive underscored that Cigar Lake will serve as a critical uranium supplier amid global nuclear energy expansion plans.

Robust geological fundamentals back the mine’s long-term value. Since entering operation, Cigar Lake has yielded a cumulative 174.5 million pounds of U3O8 uranium concentrate. Current proven reserves stand at 172.4 million pounds, supplemented by 26.3 million pounds of measured and indicated resources and another 20 million pounds of inferred resources. sum: After years of stagnation following its peak in early 2000s, nuclear energy is staging a meaningful comeback. Surging electricity demand from data centers, AI workloads and large-scale electrification, combined with energy security concerns and climate goals, is prompting governments to re-embrace nuclear as a reliable, carbon-free power source. Increased investment, innovation and supportive policies from governments will drive this new era of nuclear energy.

This global resurgence of nuclear power has put uranium under the spotlight again. The U.S. Geological Survey's inclusion of uranium on its 2025 Critical Minerals List further highlights its strategic importance for national security and domestic supply chains. Against this landscape, stocks like Cameco Corp. CCJ, Uranium Energy UEC and Centrus Energy LEU stand out as key beneficiaries of the nuclear revival.

Global electricity demand is set to rise sharply over the coming decades and nuclear power is increasingly viewed as essential to meeting that demand while keeping emissions in check. Per the World Nuclear Industry Status Report, around 65 reactors are under construction worldwide (as of Dec.5, 2025). Alongside new construction, efforts are also underway to extend the operating lives of existing reactors.

Momentum has also accelerated at the policy level. Governments across the globe have signed the Declaration to Triple Nuclear Energy, committing to triple global nuclear capacity by 2050 in recognition of nuclear power's role in energy security and climate mitigation. The World Nuclear Association estimates that global nuclear capacity could reach 1,428 GWe by 2050, surpassing the declaration's 1,200 GWe target.

The United States is aggressively pursuing nuclear independence to enhance national and energy security and reduce its heavy reliance on foreign, nuclear fuel supplies. This drive involves significant legislative action, executive orders and public-private investments aimed at revitalizing the entire domestic nuclear fuel cycle. The US is also pursuing multiple partnerships with other countries with the goal of increasing mutual nuclear development.

items.t: Trump’s Westinghouse nuclear deal comes with unresolved questions
sum: Last month, the Trump administration announced a deal to spend at least $80 billion to build at least 10 new large-scale Westinghouse reactors, a move that seemed to anoint a “national champion” in nuclear power. On its face, the agreement appeared to offer these new U.S. AP1000s — the type of reactor built at Southern Company’s Plant Vogtle in Georgia — with a guarantee of financing akin to direct funding from the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office.
But exactly how the $80 billion will be spent and when remains an open question.

The details are unusual. Rather than coming from the Energy Department, the Department of Commerce brokered the deal in what one Republican source described as an example of the administration’s internal “chaos.” Rather than coming from the federal budget, the $80 billion appears to be contingent upon Japan fulfilling its $550 billion investment in the U.S. that President Donald Trump negotiated in Tokyo last month. Rather than funneling the money through an entity such as the LPO, the disbursement process remains unclear.

“Without a sense of how this $80 billion is going to be used for nuclear in the U.S., it’s not going to give actual developers or owner-operators a chance to structure their own finances in response,” Advait Arun, a former Treasury Department analyst who now researches capital markets and energy finance at the Center for Public Enterprise think tank, told Latitude Media. “Is $80 billion going to go through LPO? Will it go through the White House? Are there other costs? There [are] all these different ways to imagine how the $80 billion will flow.”
Adding to the uncertainty, a top Energy Department official said this week the federal government may take ownership of the new reactors outright.

“The role of having the government involved in private markets is sacrosanct; you just don’t do it,” Carl Coe, the Energy Department’s chief of staff, said at a conference hosted by the Tennessee Advanced Energy Business Council. “But this is a national emergency.”

In a statement, Cameco, the Canadian uranium giant that owns a 49% stake in Westinghouse, said the initial agreement with the Trump administration set the stage to “negotiate and enter into definitive” contracts.
